n: A new message from the Lord begins—the usual way Ezekiel marks a new oracle.

f.w: the word of the LORD came unto me
f.g: This formula appears about 50 times in Ezekiel.

n: Ezekiel must turn toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them, because the hilltops were where idol worship flourished.

f.g: Ezekiel’s typical phrase for directing a prophecy at a target.

n: The whole landscape—mountains, hills, ravines, valleys—hears that God will bring a sword and destroy the “high places,” hilltop shrines for idols.

f.g: Hilltop shrines where Israelites worshiped idols or worshiped the Lord in forbidden ways.

n: Altars will be wrecked, incense stands smashed, and worshippers will die in front of the idols that could not save them.

f.g: Ezekiel’s word gillulim is a scornful term, possibly “dung-gods.”

n: Corpses and bones scattered around the altars will make these shrines unclean—an ironic end to false worship.

f.w: I will scatter your bones round about your altars

n: Every town will be ruined and every idol shrine destroyed. All the work of human hands in false worship will be wiped out.
The key refrain of Ezekiel appears: “ye shall know that I am the LORD.” It occurs over 60 times. The purpose of judgment is that people recognize who God truly is.

f.w: ye shall know that I am the LORD

n: Yet a remnant will survive and be scattered among the nations. Judgment is never God’s final word.
In exile the survivors will remember God. Strikingly, God says he is “broken” by their unfaithful hearts—he feels the pain of their betrayal. They will come to loathe their own sins.

f.g: Or “I was crushed/grieved”—God’s personal anguish over Israel’s infidelity.
A picture of covenant unfaithfulness, like a spouse who cheats.

n: They will realize God’s warnings were not empty threats.

f.w: I have not said in vain

n: Ezekiel is told to clap and stamp—gestures of grief or emphasis—and cry “Alas!” over Israel’s sins and their coming end by sword, famine, and plague.

f.w: Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot

n: No one will escape: those far away die of plague, those nearby by the sword, and those trapped in the city by famine.
The dead will lie beside the very idols they worshipped—on hilltops, under green trees and oaks, where they offered “sweet savour” to false gods instead of to the Lord.

f.g: The pleasing aroma of an offering, meant only for the Lord.

n: The land will be more desolate than the wilderness of Diblath. Then they will know the Lord.

f.g: Probably Riblah in Syria, where Zedekiah was judged; a scribal r/d confusion is likely.
